BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE

THE IDEA OF BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
America has had to educate in masses because there have been masses of people to educate. A beginning had to be made.
But masses consist of individuals and it is an implication of democracy that people shall be free to grow and develop, - be educated,- not as masses but as individuals. No matter how much it costs, no matter how long it takes we must come to this.
One side of an individual’s development has to do with individual work, with the training and imagination necessary for it.
Equally important is another side: his development through the give-and-take of responsible relations with others, through self-government, through work that requires common effort.
A community
Where people learn by contagion,
Where purpose is tested in action through daily living and goes on with daily work together,
Where there is widespread activity in the arts, making participation natural and important, is the kind of setting needed.
There experience and responsibility can be real.
There competence and control in thought, feeling, and action can be developed.
Black Mountain College is a small community concerned with the fullest development of the individuals in it. Through competence thus developed they will best be able to contribute to the well-being of society and to the scope of their own freedom.
SOME FACTS ABOUT BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
The 90 students and more than 20 faculty come from 27 states and several foreign countries. They represent a wide variation in economic and social backgrounds. The college is open to all races.
The ratio of faculty to students, being more than one-to-five, is, we believe, the highest in the country. The faculty includes a number of men internationally distinguished for original or creative work in their fields.
All candidates for graduation are examined by outside examiners, usually professors from other colleges or universities.
Black Mountain is the only college in America governed entirely by the people in it. Legal control rest with the faculty, but important responsibilities are delegated to the students, who are seriously consulted on all matters that concern them.
The admissions committee includes students as well as faculty and applicants are passed on the basis of merit, without reference to financial status. The fee is adjusted to the means of the student’s family according to a sliding scale which next year will range from a minimum of $500 to a full fee of $1600.
All students and faculty eat together and share in the practical work of keeping the place going. This means not only administrative work, but washing dishes, milking cows, clearing new land, constructing new buildings and repairing old.
The college began with 19 students and 12 teachers and their families in 1933 in rented quarters. Now with a total community of 150 settled on its own 670 acre tract, a long-range building program is envisaged as part of the educational plan for the next two decades, featured by modern planning and modern architecture.
The college is located five miles from the town of Black Mountain and 14 miles from Asheville in western North Carolina.

THE FINANCES OF BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
The College has no endowment. It would be able to operate entirely on the basis of student fees if it were not for the necessity of granting scholarships.
However, many excellent students cannot afford the full fee. Scholarships adjusted to the student’s ability to pay are therefore granted. All financial arrangements are confidential and no distinction is made in any way between students receiving aid and those who pay the full fee.

Education BMC BMC
Education at Black Mountain College is not limited to participation in classes: it penetrates the entire community life. This is the bond which unites the entire learning process and makes Black Mountain a unique adventure in the educational world. Educational practices are constantly re-evaluated and developed. Each of the faculty members is chosen not only for his facility in teaching his subject but also for his ability to participate in the administrative and community life. Students are encouraged to explore the fields of knowledge which attract them. Each faculty member acts as advisor to one to four students whom he helps choose a program suitable to the student’s needs and interests.
The classes are small; the largest has about eight members, and there are a good number of tutorials.
The natural beauty of the campus and surrounding country is an added spur to the creative activities of many students. The 600 acre campus is also a great natural laboratory were scientific methods may be studied and applied.
Black Mountain College Bulletin Volume 9 Number 3
Issued four times a year, in April, May, August and November. Entered as second class matter November 4, 1942, at the Post Office at Black Mountain, North Carolina, under the Act of August 24, 1912.

Although the curriculum is not organized exclusively toward graduation but to meet the needs of students whatever their aims may be, BMC gives a Bachelor’s Degree in Liberal Arts. Graduation is calculated in terms of achievement, not in time spent. Permission to prepare for graduation is granted a student on the basis of work completed, and written and oral tests. After successfully completing a plan of study for graduation, the student is examined by an outside examiner, chosen from the most qualified in the field of the student’s major interest.

Since Black Mountain College has no endowments, it depends almost entirely on student fees. It has tried not to eliminate anyone on the basis of his inability to pay the full fee which is $1600 an academic year (plus $13 linen fees, and a refundable contingency amount of $25). As far as the College is able, it will make reductions for particularly qualified students who could not afford to attend otherwise.

The specific classes which will be given during 1951-1952 will be organized to meet the needs and requests of the students in attendance.
In the Arts the main emphasis is on direct, full experiences with the materials. Fields represented will be: Painting, Drawing, Color and Design, Ceramics, Music, Voice, Acting and Theatre, Photography, Bookbinding, Writing, Woodshop, Printing, Weaving.
The Academic Subjects have as their purpose both the learning of systematic knowledge and the creation of a method of work. There will be courses offered in: Natural Sciences, Social Sciences, Literature, Linguistics, Languages, Mathematics, Philosophy.

A major difference from other institutions of higher learning is the degree in which students share with the faculty in all phases of college government. Students elect their own officers who preside at students meetings. The chief student officer, the Moderator, is a voting member of the faculty, and of the smaller Board of Fellows which conducts the affairs of the College.
The Community Meeting, consisting of all members of the community, governs customs, behavior and discipline. Various committees composed of students and faculty have responsibility for housing, work program, library planning, etc.
The college will continue its practice of accepting students and hiring faculty without regard to race, color and religions. There are no quotas of any sort. Students and faculty have taken an active part in opposition to the discrimination hysteria which plays such a destructive part in the life of the United States at this time.

In addition to the participation by all members of the community in keeping the College clean and in good repair, there is a voluntary program of Community Projects. These cover a wide variety of activities which permit the students to help plan and design, organize and work on new construction, remodeling, farm work, etc. Students and faculty have designed and have been the main workers on several of the living units, the large studies building, the science laboratory, and the ceramics shop.
As many students as possible are encouraged to take part in the varied activities of the college farm which supplies it with all of its meat, butter, and eggs, and some vegetables. The farm is operated for the joint purpose of producing these products and of providing students with directed experiences in the operation and management of farm work.

THE SCENE ABOVE IS A COMPOSITE OF A PORTION OF GUTZON BORGLUM’S MOUNT RUSHMORE NATIONAL MEMORIAL IN THE BLACK HILLS
Faculty architect A. Lawrence Kocher and students examine model of proposed main building. One wind has already been built, mostly by students and faculty. Kocher holds many college degrees, was head of department of architecture at Virginia and Penn State.
Black Mountain College is owned entirely by the faculty, which gives them free action. Treasurer Theodore Dreier is reporting to student-faculty group, which makes all decisions. Classes were recently closed for three days so all could help install new heating units.
Black Mountain College
A Striving Example of Democratic Education
A ringing answer to those who say that modern education is not in harmony with modern living can be found in the aims and development of Black Mountain College in western North Carolina. It was founded in 1933 by a determined band of teachers and students who felt that education must adapt the student to the community and the community to the student, so that citizens would live, not by absorbed rules, but by a practical understanding of what the citizen and the community owe each other.
The college is small, but it was designed and built almost entirely by the labor of the faculty and students. No grades and no rigid courses of study are required, yet Black Mountain students are admitted to such august bodies as the Harvard Graduate School. In a multitude of ways, Black Mountain demonstrates the basic and vital truth that real democracy is a living, dynamic force.
PHOTOGRAPHS BY MICHAEL LEVELLE FOR FRIENDS MAGAZINE
No athletics at Black Mountain, but plenty of healthy and fruitful work as students help built their own college. Every student must join in some practical work. Sometimes professional artisans are called in from nearby towns, when work is too skilled for students to do. But they dig ditches, mix cement, hammer and saw. Secretaries work in building that was a summer lodge, pending better quarters. Betty Mosley (left) was secretary to mayor of Dallas, now works for college treasurer.
Robert Babcock conducts class in political science. Classes are so small that every student gets near-tutor attention. There are no grades, no required courses.
Cardinal principle at Black Mountain is no fraternities or other groups where money or social position matters. College holds dances twice each week; all join.
Ingenious Paco Leon makes more room for daytime by designing a bed that raises out of the way. He spent most of his life in Spain, is interested in radio engineering.
Living quarters are cramped, but all fare alike. Each student shares sleeping quarters but has private study. Tuition is $400-$1200, depending on ability to pay. Students do not know what other have paid, so all rank as equals. All keep own rooms neat.
This is completed wing of model shown on opposite page. By helping to build it, all have learned to cooperate, have greater appreciation of value of community effort. College has twenty instructors, only 75 students; hopes to raise that to about 125.
So ingrained in the spirit of democracy that work does not have to be assigned; the first on in the dining room, student or teacher, begins serving food. Connie Spencer balances seven cups. Each tried to out-balance others, but broke too many dishes.
How FRIENDLY are you? THIS TEST WILL TELL YOU
PHOTOGRAPHS BY BLACK BOX STUDIOS FOR FRIENDS MAGAZINE
The ability to make and hold friends is admittedly a business and social asset of first importance. For readers who would like to test their friendliness, FRIENDS has prepared a brief yet comprehensive set of test questions, in cooperation with Dr. Donald A. Laird, Ph. D., Sci. D., who is nationally known for his work and lectures in the psychological field. Among his many books are How to Make People Like You and How to Use Psychology in Business. Dr. Laird directed the Psychological Laboratories at Colgate University for 14 years. The questions on these pages were prepared by him and offer an indicative, though not absolute, guide to your ability to win and hold friends. Just answer an honest “Yes” or “No” to each question, then find your score on page 21. But don’t take it too seriously- remember that no general test works perfectly for everybody, and low score should not upset you. A low score should, however, make you ask yourself why…for your friends’ sake!

Chase Osborn acts as his own weather man, has two barometers at Possum Polk, his Georgia winter home. His daily readings of weather conditions are kept in diary.
Although 82, former Governor Osborn leads an active life, rising at five a.m., and personally overseeing every detail of plantation. He summers in north Michigan.
Key reason for his amazing health is daily quota of 12 quarts of “Lake Superior” water. He has analyzed his water supply, finds it identical with Lake Superior.
Friends visit CHASE OSBORN the “Iron Hunter” of Possum Polk
The lusty whoop of delight is in praise of some especially good dish served by Lee, his cook. Guests are served liberally, but if they do not eat everything, portions are smaller next time. Chase Osborn even saves soap slivers. “It may mean a few pennies more for charity,” he explains.
Each afternoon, the Governor hauls down the American flag and renders a prayer asking God’s blessing on the people of the United States. He also raises flag each day.
Democratic and truly interested in everyone, the Governor chats with two field hands. He is a sound scholar; in 1939 added 40,000 statistical square miles to Michigan showing that former tabulations had failed to include American portion of Great Lakes.
Several dozen letter a day come to Chase Osborn, and he personally answers all. His daughter, Stellanova, serves as secretary. He puts in a ten-hour working day. This is in line with his maxim: “Apply your principles thoroughly and do no slight small things.”
A fabulous character indeed is Charles Salmon Osborn, one time-Governor of Michigan, intimate friend of Presidents, who rose from a log cabin to the heights, and has returned to a log cabin for the rich final years of his life. Known as the “Iron Hunter,” for the ore-prospecting that earned him many millions of dollars, he gave away nearly all his possessions, now lives quietly at Possum Polk in Possum Lane, Poulan, Georgia, in the winter; spends the summers at Duck Island in Michigan’s St. Mary’s River. He is 82, but still rises at five a.m., does a full day’s work before retiring early in the evening.
“My greatest inheritance was poverty,” says this wise man of his early life in an Indiana log cabin. “It was bitter, but poverty is ambition’s stepladder. With money came reflection. I saw the earth as a vast banquet table, with plenty for all if each would take a fair share, but some were taking more than they needed and others were going hungry. I decided to give back all I had that I did not need to live on. People who are blessed with a surplus should think of themselves as trustees for those who have nothing, and help them up to the table. That day is coming; it is not charity, it is Christian justice.”
Chase Osborn practiced what he preaches. His millions went to churches, charities and schools. And at 82 he is happy, healthful, beloved by his friends, brimming with zest for life. Of thrift, he says, “The best way to save is not to spend.”
PHOTOGRAPHS BY BETTY TRUXELL FOR FRIENDS MAGAZINE
The faultless manners of Governor Osborn, a gentleman of the old school, delight his guests. He seats them all, bows to each in turn, then renders grace with a beautiful prayer. The guest house is Big Polk; his smaller working quarters, Little Polk.
Blessed with a multitude of friends, great and small, Osborn remembers them all. He is mailing sacks of pecans as Christmas gifts. His friends have included nine Presidents.
When the Governor wishes solitude, he retires to the attic at Little Polk and pulls stairway up behind him- his own invention, and an ingenious one. Viola Hardage watches.
Carry-over from pioneering days, when his prospecting for iron ore earned him the name “Iron Hunter,” Osborn keeps loaded revolver in his simply-furnished bedroom.

In Indiana high school basketball, long, rangy boys, such as Jim Riffey, who takes the jump from Merle Horrall, his substitute, are the rule.
Basic factor in Indiana’s ranking as top basketball state is attention given to getting youths interested early and keeping them that way. Marion Crawley, high school coach, finds nothing strange in giving regular pointers to nine-to-thirteen-year-olds such as these. They ask sharp questions, too.
Basketball is America’s Biggest Sport and its home is Indiana
Asked to pick America’s favorite sport, most fans might single out basketball, or possibly football, for the crown. Paid attendance, however, tells a different story. Judged entirely by the number of people who lay down hard cash to see what happens, basketball, with more than 80,000,000 paid admission annually, leads the pack. Basketball is a half-century old this winter. In January 1891, a Y.M.C.A. official at Springfield, Mass., Dr. James A. Naismith, called some boys together and explained a new game he had a new game he had thought up, involving tossing a ball through peach baskets nailed several feet above the floor. From that time on, basketball climbed steadily upward in the number and interest of its fans. Few observers today would deny that basketball’s true home is in Indiana high schools. Indianians are not fans- they are basketball-crazy. In town after town in Hoosierdom the gym or coliseum where basketball is played is the town’s largest and finest building. Each year there is a state tournament at Indianapolis, and 15,000 rabid fans jam Butler University field house to cheep the home-town boys. Potential players are watched anxiously from grade school days, and any six-footer not out for his school team had better tell why. Last year’s champions were the Hatchets, of Washington, Ind. (pop. 10,000). Herewith, a quick glimpse of the system that produces the high school teams for which Indiana is justly (and lustily) famed.
Don’t be too sure this is a gag picture. The young man is Coach Crawley’s year-old son, and Crawley takes no chances on player shortages.
When the Washington, Ind., team won the 1941 state championship, madness swept the town. Bonfires, parades, banquets were order of day.
The current edition of Washington’s defending high school champions pays close heed to Coach Crawley as he charts an offensive maneuver on the gym floor. Nearly 800 Indiana high schools participate in basketball competition. Washington has won crown twice since 1931.
Washington offers little in the way of gay night life, and all players are proverbially broke, so a “coke date” is standard. Hook Mangin with Joyce McCafferty, and Art Grove with Doris McKay, have fun without breaking training, in Williams’ Drug Store.
Tense moment in one of last year’s state tournament games, when the Hatchets tamed the Kokomo Wildcats, went on to the championship. Butler’s large field house is scene of these games, and its 15,000 capacity is regularly strained. Emphasis in Indiana is on “racehorse” or “firewagon” tactics, built around speed, stamina, fast-breaking offense.
Practice, practice, and still more practice, is the rule at Washington. It averages three hours a day, five days a week. Washington is a town of 10,000; gym seats 4,000.
Taking no chances that his Hatchets might lose their sharpness, Coach Crawley invited his first team to live at his house for the four weeks of 1941 tournament play.
Hook Mangin, star of last year’s champions, at dinner with mother and best girl Joyce McCafferty. Dads of all five varsity members work at local B & O railroad shops.
No different from other American youngsters, Art and Doris are adapt jitterbugs. Indiana high schools produce more college All-Americans than any other state.
Highlights of the show are impersonations by Mickey and Judy. Mickey takes to blackface for his impression of Mr. Tambo, who “plays banjo like Eddie Peabody.” He’s good.
Show-stopper is Mickey as Carmen Marooney, a hilarious song-and-dance routine. Mickey spends two and a half hours putting on make-up and costume for this parody.
“Just a wee drap and dorrach,” says this member of the Highland clan of MacRooney’s, as Mickey gives forth with a great impersonation of the beloved Sir Harry Lauder.
“Spaghetti with a song” is what Jack Lipsom is getting in this scene as he uneasily listens to a serenade by Mickey, Ray MacDonald (left) and Richard Quine. In the picture they are “The Three Balls of Fire-Once We’re Started You Can’t Put Us Out.”
With the double barreled idea od raising money for an orphanage outing and gaining the interest of a Broadway producer, Mickey, Judy and Virginia Weidler get orphanage director Donald Meek to let them stage benefit show, Then the action is on!
America’s next dance fad should be the Hoe-Down, if the energy displayed by Mickey and Judy in reviving this streamlined version of it can make it so. It has all that the most jittery jitterbug could ask in the way of jumping and jiving. Good stuff.
Tragedy rears its head when the building rented for the benefit show is condemned as unsafe. Mickey sadly announces the fact, but the audience leaves without taking back its money, and the producer sees the show as a special performance.
Mickey Rooney and Judy Garland RETURN IN “BABES ON BROADWAY”
Friend’s Movie of the Month by Dick Francis
A movie success-formula that has proved its potency twice already is being revived in the picture Babes on Broadway. That formula is to team together Mickey Rooney and Judy Garland, add plenty of music, lots of songs, a plot that doesn’t have to do much more than keep up with the cast, and there you have it. Just such concoctions were Babes in Arms and Strike Up the Band, and both were the box office’s best friend. Busby Berkeley, who took care of directing the first two, is back on the job again, so how can you go wrong?
As you might expect, Babes on Broadway is a merry little bauble of entertainment that moves without limping, from comedy to pathos to trickery to self-sacrifice, and smoothly up to a happy ending. Rooney’s incredibly expressive face and rather explosive brand of likeableness have full opportunity to hold sway, and Judy is once again the talented nice girl who brings him to his senses at just the right moment. There are several front-row tunes, one of the best being How About You? Which Judy dshes out with gusto and assurance.
Plot never means a great deal in these Rooney-Garland get-togethers, and all you need to know is that the story deals with the plight of talented young hopefuls who have a great yearning to see their names in Broadway lights but have a good many problems in getting them there. In this case, a benefit show seems the best way to attract the eye of producer Thornton Reed, capably played by James Gleason. Mickey is all set to run out on the scheme, but Judy’s scorn reforms him and it all works out beautifully for everybody.
Judy Garland does her share of impersonations to keep pace with Mickey. This one is of the great Sarah Bernhardt, Judy also does an encore of her famous Franklin D. Roosevelt Jones.
Fay Templeton is remembered by millions- Judy imitates her singing of Mary’s a Grand Old Name. impersonations are inspired by old billboards as they rehearse in long-unused theater.

Bicycle-soccer
Bicycle-Soccer demands quick headwork, and here Ilo Lorenz uses her head to advance the ball, much to the alarm of Mary Cheseboro. Hands may not touch ball.
Plenty of spills, but no one was hurt. To distinguish teams, one wears colored halter-aprons. Here, Virginia Butler, Adel Heiden pedal past spilled Peggy Sargent.
As in all sports, team members and spectators are on hand to cheer their favorites. Ilo Lorenz whoops it up for her side; an impromptu cheering section added their voices.
Goalee Dorothy Wilson drops her bike, goes high in the air to block an attempted goal. Goalees alone are allowed to use hands on the ball, but on most scoring tries, it is surer and easier to simply block the ball with extended bicycle.
Game starts when referee puts ball in play by throwing it between teams. Object, as in regular soccer, is to propel ball past opponents’ goal line. Mrs. Catharine Sample, director of girls’ athletics at Ponce de Leon, acts as referee. Players use their own bicycles.
Action-to-spare is the rule in this picture, as Muriel Smith (far right) pedals madly into position to cut off the ball from Ann Cone (center), who has dismounted to block it. Florida students, long accustomed to year-round outdoor sports, have great stamina.
Time-out while the Whites plan strategy. Balmy Florida climate makes shorts both practical and comfortable. Shown left to right, Helen Tomlinson, Betty Ellis, Muriel Smith, Gloria Harpe, Lucene Gordon and Peggy Sargant rest, argue, plan tactics.
May be America’s Next Sport Craze
A new sport that seems to have all the elements that make any game popular is bicycle-soccer. Action, thrills, spills, teamwork- this game has them all. Pictures on these pages were made at Ponce de Leon High School, at Coral Gables, Florida, where climate, athletically-minded students and habitual use of bicycles provide a natural setting for one of the nation’s newest games. Basic rules are the same as for soccer, with variations to fit the needs of playing on bicycles rather than on foot. Also, instead of the usual eleven-man team, bicycle-soccer teams seem to work better with an abbreviated six-man team, to cut down confusion and chances of collision.
As in soccer, players are not permitted to touch ball with their hands (except the goalees), but have the added advantage of being able to block the ball with their bicycles. Rules provide that players may not dismount to kick the ball toward goal, but must have one leg on each side of the bicycle. TRANSPLANTING A TOWN New Englanders Move Entire Village to New Location
U.S. Army engineers decided to build a flood control dam in the valley of the Pemigewasset River, near Franklin, N.H. this project would have doomed the village of Hill, located in the area to be flooded, had not the villagers decided to move en masse.
Led by Selectmen Theodore Dickerson, Edward Amsden and John Huse, the townspeople worked out all details of planning and financing the moving of Hill to its new location. To assure related architectural design, an Association, in complete control, was formed.
When the Federal Government decided to build a flood control dam at Franklin, New Hampshire, it put the village of Hill literally in the middle. Hill was in the middle of the valley to be flooded, and might have been expected to follow the example of other towns, which simply went out of existence when faced with similar problems. The townspeople decided, however, that they liked one another well enough to tackle the problem of moving the entire village a quarter-mile west, to higher ground, so that their town would still be an entity. For good measure, they decided to make the new village “New England’s Model Town,” with planning and architecture worked out to make it the best-looking, most livable town in the region. Led by the village selectmen, they worked out ways and means of financing the civic cost involved, and did most of the moving and rebuilding work themselves. They became so excited over the idea that they erected this sign,
NOW APPROACHING THE VILLAGE OF HILL NEW HAMPSHIRE
TO BE MOVED TO NEW SITE ¼ MILLE WEST AS RESULT OF FRANKLIN FLOOD CONTROL DAM
To Be New England’s Model Town
PHOTOGRAPHS BY DAN STILES FOR FRIENDS MAGAZINE
George Mason, who deals in antiques, was made head of the Hill Village Improvement Association. It controls land use and house plans. Half-acre lots are $100-200.
Carpenter A. Howard Wilson, lifelong Hill resident, helped many of his neighbors to plan and build their new homes. New village has only one general store.
First Selectman Theodore S. Dickerson, one of the leaders in planning details of new village, is a farmer. Here he gets on with storing his supply of winter firewood.
Houses that could be re-designed to conform to the architecture of the new village were moved in the old-fashioned New England way- two horses operating windlasses providing power. About 75 families live in Hill. Only a dozen houses were moved.
Most houses and other buildings in the old village were left to the wreckers, and brand-new ones built on the new site. The villagers are proud of their new town hall (shown in contrast with the old), which contains auditorium, library, fire station.
All the housewives are enthusiastic- and no wonder- over the spick-and-span new homes and kitchens. Mrs. Charles Willard likes her kitchen especially well. All homes, stores and factories, present and future, are to be similarly modern colonial in design.
Main street in the old village was typical of small New England towns, with all buildings lined along one main street. There was no harmony of house or building design. The residents determined to correct faults in their new town site.
STREETS IN THE NEW VILLAGE ARE BROAD AND CURVING, WITH AMPLE SPACE FOR FLOWER BEDS. IT EPITOMIZES THE BEST AND GENUINE SPIRIT OF NEW ENGLAND.

Pop Shaffer’s Animals Grow On Trees
PHOTOGRAPHS BY CHARLES HERBERT FOR FRIENDS MAGAZINE
Clem Shaffer, known as “Pop” to all his neighbors in Mountainair, New Mexico, is a prime example of a man who does just what he wants to do. Sixty-odd, Pop is a blacksmith by trade, owns a hotel that provides his living and leaves him free to follow his engrossing hobby-the creation of Rancho Bonita, stocked with wild animals of weird and wonderful forms, all made from nature’s own materials, just polished a bit.
Gnarled tree trunks and branches, roots, stumps and rocks are Pop’s raw material. What he does is use a boundless and lively imagination to see in these twisted forms a resemblance to some wild animal. Carving away the surplus twigs, etc., and putting them out to weather for a year, he has created more than 150 of these creatures, hopes to complete a thousand before he finishes. People who have seen the “ranch” are amazed at the results. Pop has already spent $10,000 on his zoo, but none of his animals are for sale. It is a hobby pure and simple, and a tourist attraction that always amazes visitors.
In his workshop at Mountaineer, New Mexico, Pop Shaffer puts the finishing touches on one of the queer, animal-like forms his quick eye saw in a part of some tree’s formation.
Last year, more than 12,000 tourists visited his Rancho Bonita, where more than 150 of his completed animals are on display. He says they’re the ones Noah wouldn’t take in the ark.
Children as well as adults are fascinated and delighted by the strange denizens of Pop Shaffer’s wooden zoo. Little Betty Jo Tabet thinks this one to eat from her hand.
This remarkable caricature of an elk, by nature, with Pop serving only as “spotter” of her handiwork, is typical of the strange sights visitors see. He hopes to create many more.
Only Pop Shaffer would have seen a lion’s mane in a tree trunk surrounded by a fungus growth. Properly located branches serve as legs, a scraggly branch for a tail. Pop sawed out a mouth, added realistic teeth- and a fearsome yet instantly recognizable king of beasts is the result. Pop retired from business in 1937, devotes full time to hobby.

STUDENTS AND FACULTY HAVE DESIGNED AND CONSTRUCTED THE MAIN STUDY BUILDING OF BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
INFORMAL CLASSES are usual at the college. Students wear casual work clothes, girls prefer to roll their blue jeans or else wear shorts. Classes are held in the Main Studies building or in faculty homes. Here, Prof. Strauss conducts discussion in philosophy.
INDIVIDUAL STUDY ROOMS are allotted each student in the Main Building. The rooms are furnished by the students, used to work after classes. The faculty have similar studies to use for their own projects. The students do not sleep here but live in dorms.
The College That Built Itself
Black Mountain points its program to the future
Ten years ago, a group of rebellious educators pooled their resources and went back into the mountains of western North Carolina to found a new kind of college. They were men who opposed the study courses and graduation credit system existing in most American universities. They were dissatisfied with standard methods of teaching. They felt that higher education had lost its basic purpose- to train students for leadership in the nation as well as a job in life.
The result was Black Mountain College, an experiment in education, a blueprint for democracy at work. It’s a college which has been built, in main, by its students and faculty and not by financial grants and endowments.
Despite chronic financial crises, Black Mountain continues to grow in reputation as well as in size, although it has not prospered. In the post-war world, this college may take the lead in pointing the way to a new type of training for our youth.
If the war is to mean anything, it must lead the way to a greater regard of man for his fellow-man. Paradoxically, that job begins on the battlefields of the world. But it must also be done in the schools and colleges. To educate is not enough. Youth must be trained in cooperation and democracy.
Black Mountain tries to do the job in two ways. It educates through an interrelated program of subjects where the influence of history on literature is covered in a single course, where philosophy and the social sciences become a study of man’s problems in the terms of the student’s own experiences. It trains through a work program which teaches students the proper use of tools, gives them a community sense and responsibility about their work.
When the faculty and students first came to Black Mountain, it had a few small buildings, formerly part of a summer hotel, which inadequately housed the college. Since then, both faculty and students participating in the work program have constructed twelve buildings, cultivated a farm, built tennis courts. They designed the plans, cut the lumber, formed the cement blocks for their modern main study building. In blue jeans and work clothes, piling into college trucks, the students and teachers together built a college where no college had been.
That the program of Black Mountain has been successful is evident in the way students speak about the college. Twenty-one-year-old Bob Marden, a senior, sums it up this way:
“You change when you come here. It may take a long time; it may take three or four days. But after a while you feel the community spirit here and soon you start saying, ‘we built this and we did that’!”
Persons who talk like that know what democracy means. They know it means freedom buy they also know it mean responsibility.
Black Mountain is not a rich man’s college nor does it pay high salaries to its faculty. Less than 50 per cent of the students pay the full fee of $1200 for room, board and tuition. In the past ten years, the college annually has allotted $30,000 of its limited budget for scholarships. You can’t “work your way through” Black Mountain. But if the faculty admissions committee believes in your ability, the tuition scale can slide down to nothing.
When the faculty of a college votes to take new salary cuts- as they did at Black Mountain- while increasing the scholarship fund, then you know you’ve found a school which can’t die, a school which will continue to build itself into a highly important institution.
STUDENTS BEGIN CLEARING LAND FOR A NEW PROJECT
CONCERTS, ART EXHIBITIONS, guest lectures are held frequently in the college dining hall which is converted into a grand salon for special occasions. Plays are presented here by the college group. Saturday nights students and faculty hold a semi-formal dance.
40 41
THE COLLEGE THAT BUILT ITSELF continued
W. ROBERT WUNSCH ELSA KAHL THEODORE DREIER HEINRICH JALOWETZ
KENNETH KURTZ A. LAWRENCE KOCHER JOSEF ALBERS FRITZ J. HANSGIRG
Outstanding Men and Women Staff the College
W. ROBERT WUNSCH, college rector, is administrative head elected by the faculty. One of the original founders, Wunsch teaches dramatics, is an authority on Negro educational problems in the South. KENNETH KURTZ gives English and American literature. A former Rhodes scholar, he previously taught at Cal. Tech. ELSA KAHL, leading director of the Ballet Jooss, came to teach “eukinetics”- a study of motion-when ballet disbanded last year. Her husband, Frederic Cohen, ballet music director, also teaches. A. LAWRENCE KOCHER, one of America’s top architects, has courses in design, supervises all college construction. THEODORE DREIER, also one of the original group which founded Black Mountain College in 1933, teaches mathematics, was formerly at Rollins College. JOSEF ALBERS, art professor, taught at the Bauhaus, Germany, until its closing by Hitler. He is assembling a color exhibit of college work for Museum of Modern Art. HEINRICH JALOWETZ, one of pre-Nazi Europe’s outstanding conductors, teaches music composition and form at the college. FRITZ J. HANSGIRG, professor of physical sciences, was paroled by FBI to college after war broke. Classified as enemy alien, he was designing magnesium plants for Henry Kaiser.
A HUNDRED-ACRE FARM, tilled by volunteer labor of students and professors, supplies the college with vegetables, milk, and some meat. It is an integral part of the practical work program which teaches students responsibility to the community and familiarity with everyday work tools. College work program varies from construction, pasture clearance, and road repair to electric wiring, cabinet making. Students put in three days each week on the work program. Since no student can pay for tuition by working, the program has a real educational value.
“WERKLEHRE” is what Professor Albers calls his classes in art design. Students have an unlimited choice of materials- textiles, leaves, paints- to develop an understanding of the subject. Like almost all other courses of study at Black Mountain College, art classes are flexible, do not confine themselves solely to one phase of art. Weaving looms in foreground of photo are used both for practical work and design study.
LABORATORY EQUIPMENT and scientific apparatus is used by students for elementary work in physics and undergraduate work in chemistry and biology. Equipment is housed in long, one-story wooden building built by the students. Science department is concentrating on war work.
POST-WAR PLANNING CLASSES are not confined to social studies but include practical work in architecture. Here, designer Kocher explains the model for a post-war pre-fabricated home which can be constructed for $1500 on a mass production scale. Classes at college are usually small.

Reprinted from Arts and Decoration, January, 1935
ART AS A FOURTH “R”
A NEW AMERICAN COLLEGE IS COMBATING THE IDEA THAT ONLY PAINTERS CAN PAINT
THE point of growth in any country is along its frontiers. After a land is scattered with masonry and fences, most of its frontiers are mental.
Changing attitudes toward art have been for months faintly discernible in American distances. But not too faintly for me to want to investigate when I heard rumors of a new college in North Carolina where art was said to be exciting otherwise normal healthy students.
I went to the Blue Ridge Mountains to live for a week and go to classes with students of Black Mountain College.
The mood of this new college was established under the leadership of Professor John Andrew Rice. He has a theory that there are two kinds of men today, the Renaissance man and the modern man. By his definition, practically all the graduates of well bred Eastern colleges emerge as Renaissance men. Their minds are furnished with a set of ideas- some from the classics, from history, from mathematics. Mr. Rice doesn’t think this is enough for the modern man.
On the theory that life is by necessity a moving, changing thing demanding action as well as thinking, this school is organized around the practical uses and appreciation of art as the only force which can bring emotions into disciplined relation to thought. The aim is eventually to get through art a common experience for people- something which they mutually can talk about aside from clothes and eating and drinking.
The curriculum of this college, in outline not different from the curriculum of other institutions of higher learning, provides a unique opportunity for students to acquaint themselves with art subjects. There are no required courses. The student acquaints himself with the fields of knowledge, and then makes a selection of the things he personally wants most to know.
The process of exposing the student’s mind to art is done entirely by indirection. At the hours when important art courses are being conducted, no other classes are held, so that any student may enroll without conflict. Further, the student’s own interest in art classes spreads the interest in painting through the school.
Mr. Rice feels that American art schools are still working too much on the principle of self expression, that the arts should merge and make a respectable place in the realistic world. “It is unfortunate that so many graduates are held to their colleges by writing as a sort of umbilical cord. Like Socrates’ demon who told him what not to do, the college should cut away the false illusions the student has about himself and his own abilities and reveal to him possible adjustments which can make fit into a possible world. The college should be a complete world in itself, a perfection of the outside world. The experience in the college should have the same quality as experiences of the outside world.”
It was in the hope of building a college like this that he established a democratic community at Black Mountain. Men and women students and faculty live in the same dormitory and eat together three times a day. They maintain an independent community as naturally and successfully as did large families on the American frontier.
Indeed, I was not sure as I arrived that I had not struck the lost American Frontier itself. We met as we drove into the fate that starts a steep ascent to the college buildings, an overalled girl student with a shotgun on her shoulder.
“Betsy’s hunting bears again,” the student driver said over his shoulder. Betsy, pampered offspring of a socially prominent family, happens to like to go off hunting alone, hoping to meet a bear. (She hasn’t met one yet, but if she did, she’d probably take it calmly.)
After Betsy and the bears, chronologically, met next surprise at Black Mountain College was Plato. It went around by word of mouth that there was to be a Plato seminar the evening of my arrival. The tone of voice (anticipation- could it be?) moved me to debate attending. I went. So, to my amazement, did fifteen or twenty other people who were not enrolled in the course. Classes are not regarded as a bore at Black Mountain.
In most American colleges, the school of fine arts is regarded as the remote, gifted sister of the school. Except for a few courses in history and theory, we ordinary citizens emerged from college into life without the vaguest idea that participating in creative art had anything to do with us.
The courses in art which Professor Josef Albers teaches at Black Mountain College are, surprisingly, not for artists but for people. Art becomes a discipline and focusing of personal powers, and a release for original creation.
There are classes in drawing and color and Werklehre,
1 OVER
The development of the feeling for material and space. The student acquaints himself with wood and glass and tin and various plastics. He does not copy existing forms in these materials, but works with the material from his own fresh, original point of view, as the designer must learn to do. There are no answers in the back of the book for the problems Professor Albers gives in this course. The right answer for each student is his individual acquaintance with a material- its properties and limitations, and his imaginative use of that experience to build up new forms. A few designers may emerge from these classes. But every student is sure to feel the discipline of this creative thinking.
It is a standing joke that the only course that was originally intended to be exclusively for students majoring in fine arts, is attended by nearly everyone in the college, students and faculty. title: Ice Meadows
credit: Gift of the Artist
description:
Pillar of imperfect clear rectangle on top of gray rectangular base.

An ice meadow is a naturally occurring phenomenon that involves floating pieces of ice in the winter months to be washed up on shore and remain there until spring. The ice acts as a natural barrier to tree growth and helps to deposit organic materials on the shore that promote the growth of smaller plants. When a river is polluted, this natural process is threatened.

This work was inspired by a frozen lake, fed by the Cuyahoga River, that the artist and a friend visited during a teaching stint in Cleveland, Ohio. Polluted by the dumping of industrial waste, the Cuyahoga River famously catches fire, a fact Bernstein references in the polished section of the glass, where the water appears to flow rather than freeze. He was not only bringing attention this type of terrain, he was also commenting on environmentalism and the importance of a healthy river.

This was not the first time that river was part of a conversation about pollution and the environment. In fact a photograph of the Cuyahoga River on fire in 1969 was put on the cover of Time magazine and gained national attention. This focus on the health of our planet inspired the first Earth Day in 1970 and helped to pass The Clean Water Act of 1972.

[Source: Lola Clairmont & Museum Staff]

title: BMC typed class notes on isotints
description:
Ostwald arranges his colors in a double-cone solid with an axis of gradations from white to black. (eight, including black and white) These he calls the non-chromatic colors and like Munsell he recognizes black and white as COLOR, which psychologically is true, through for the physicists, whose medium is light, black remains the absence of all color and white and presence of all color.
Around the equator of the solid he arranged 24 CHROMATIC colors (full color with no black or white content) eight of which are primary colors.. yellow, orange, red, violet, U-Blue, Ice blue, sea green, leaf green. Each chromatic color has eight steps in equidistance to top apex(a) white; these are known as the light-clear series. The eight steps towards bottom apex (p) black are known as the dark-clear series..
The greys are equidistant and proceed in geometrical progression. They are labelled a, c, e, g, I, l, n, p.
The 24 chromatic are also psychologically equidistant, but unlike the greys they do not have finite end points such as black are known as the dark-clear series.
Non chromatic colors… white to black
Chromatic colors.. full, spectrum colors
Light clear series… steps toward white
Dark clear series… steps toward black
Monochromatic triangles.. a half of a cross section of the cone shows all the possibilities of one color.
Isotints..steps parallel to lower side of triangle which have the same white content as the grays from which they rise obliquely upward
Isotones..steps parallel to upper side of triangle which have the same black content as the grays from which descend obliquely downward.
(isotints and isotones cross each other in every color in the triangle and may be remembered as having their origin in the gray axis)
Shadow series… Parallel steps in the triangle to the axis of the solid, the black content increases progressively downwards as in gray series while the amount of full color is constant.
Isovalent circles… these result from cutting the cone horizontally There are 28 in all, one for each color in the monochromatic triaangle. All colors in a given circle contain same amount of black white aand full color therefore are of equal value, hence their name..isovalent.
(note) non chromatic colors can be changed only in one way, that is they can be made lighter or darker but chromatic colors can be modified in four ways. 1. A red can be made more yellow or more blue, a blue redder or greener and so on (equator)
2. The hue may be retained and white added to make it progressively lighter (light clear series)
3. the hue may be retained and black added to make it progressively darker (dark clear series)
4. The hue may be retained and black and white added to make the color progressively grayer (monochromatic triangle)

title: Black Mountain College class notes on Geothe's Theory and Schopenhauer's Theory
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Geothe's Theory
The greatest contrast possible lies between blue and yellow, known as the proto-contrast. Yellow is the lightest possible color, blue the dark, Red, having both light and dark qualities is intermediary.
complementary colors are found by reading from one vertex to the opposite side.
The three remaining colors are tertiary colors.
Schopenhauer's theory
Here, the basic difference from Geothe is in the division of color according to a balance of light. Yellow is the lightest possible color, violet the darkest, therefore, in a color wheel which has been divided into 36 parts the total number of parts occupied by yellow and violet (12) are divided.. or three is given to yellow and the remainder 9 is given to violet.
Orange and blue.... the 12 parts are devided into thirds, oranges gets 4 blue gets 8.
Red and green.. they are equally devided as they are equal in color and light
(this color wheel does not allow for black white or grays

title: BMC class notes on hues, value, and chroma
description:
Munsell.. Divides color into tree dimensions of quality: hue, value and chroma.
Hue- name of color related to wave lengths
Value- understandable only in relation to black and white (light intensity)
Chroma- color intensity, degree of saturation of color
The initial color wheel of his solid or tree is composed of 10 colors (hue) red, yellow red, yellow, green yellow, green, blue green, blue, purple blue, purple, red purple. Complimentary colors are diametrically opposite.
In the color “tree” colors are arranged vertically according to value, horizontally according to chroma. Value distinguishes a lighter from a darker color and matches this quality to the corresponding step on the gray scale. Chroma distinguishes colors by their strength in an even progression outward from the central gray scale. Here lies the initial difference between the Munsell and the Ostwald.. Ostwald arranges his colors in a solid double cone, the top cone colors going towards white, the bottom towards black. It is not possible to add new colors. Munsell’s colors are arranged from the central ‘gray-scale’ axis and proceed outwards.. some colors extending farther than others (such as the colors to which he gives more range than others.. red, red yellow.. whereas violet and yellow consist of very short ‘branches’. This is supposed to be an advantage over the Ostwald system. Actually it is not possible to add more colors than are present in the Ostwald system (it includes the whole known or knowable spectrum) expect perhaps full hues of more brilliancy.
The greatest advantage of Ostwald’s or Munsells system is that they bring a kind of order into the names and identification of colors.. a distinct help for printers textile manufacters etc. Munsell’s names are given in fractions.. such as BLUEGREEN 7/4 would be blue green in the 7th step of the value and the 4th step of chroma. (there are in all 398 colors, nine greys and black and white)

258 East Mountain Drive
Santa Barbara, CA 93109
January 1, 1988
Dear Ati:
I am writing to invite you to contribute to a collection of Black Mountain College tales. Do you have a recollection or two that you think is indicative of your experience there, and that you tell your children or friends about life at BMC? How/Why did BMC influence your life? WHo did or said something that strongly affected you, and what were the circumstances?
Three books on Black Mountain have been published. There is Fee Dawson's book, which has the vitality of being personal and subjective. The Duberman and Harris book, excellent both in their own ways, have been the work of scholars, cultural historians, relying on research, interviews artifacts and documentation.
What these books miss out on is the composite texture of what we underwent and shared there, all the impressions we experienced apart from tutelage, under tutelage, and despite and in defiance of tutelage. *There was more going on than the incubation of cultural heros,!
I believe a book of accounts, anecdotes, vignettes written by host of BMC students and teachers would tap into the human component that was part of the College as everyday life, and at an intriguing time in our personal histories. An anthology of stories is likely to be filled with suprises, delights, experiences we didn't realize at the time, or knew and forgot. The collection would capture the currents and nuances missing from the pedgogic, communitarian and artistic emphases hitherto published.
There is no one theme I would impose upon this solicitation. I mean it to be open so that the final compilation will generate its own stands of significance, its own configurations, energy, and center. I am writing approximately 100 people, to begin with, Out of that number, which I hope will grow (see #4 below), an anthology will be put together. If the idea pleases you, and you are interested in contributing to this Black Mountain collection, please send me as soon as possible:
1) Your written piece or pieces (story, anecdote, tale, account- 2,000 words or less)
2) A short bio/vita, with the years you attended BMC; and any photos you might have (glossy, b/w) of yourself, other people (please identify), and BMC scenes
3) Any stipulations or conditions or requests you wish to see carried out by me (the editor)
4) The names and addresses of several BMC people whom you think would like to contribute a tale or two.
Wishing you the very best in the New Year and, in the spirit of this undertaking, hoping to hear from you soon, I am Cordially, Merv Lane - BMC 1946-48

dear Slats deat faraway Slats!
out of sight all these years, but never really out of mind! Always hoping still to get news of you and yours, (but never able to get to the west coast) I send you this so that you'll understand why Charles, Moly and others, I so particularly missed you recently!
Well, there was this reunion at Bard College in April..... (see enclosed momentoes). It served, for some 50 old B.M.C.ers, who were able to get to it, as an almost excruciatingly vivid and short reminder of that place, and that time. It's crazy actuality, its genuinness, its induplicatable vitality all became believable again for a few hours, and let us see it afresh.
WE WERE LUCKY. THE EVENING WAS PURE SPRING THE FRENSH DOORS OF THE OLD MANSION OPEN WIDE. THE LAWNS RUNNING DOWN TO THE HUDSON RIVER GREEN AND WARM. WE GATHERED IN A ROOM FILLED WITH BALLOONS. THE SOUND OF EVARTS MUSIC (ON TAPE) AND THE LIVE PIANO OF JUDD WOLDIN. AND TALKED, AND TALKED, AND ATE AND ATE, AND DANCED AND TOASTED UNFORGETTABLE NAMES WITH NEVER-ENDING CHAMPAGNE.
The B.M.C. exhibit @ the gallery, next door as well as the amazingly comprehensive book "THE ARTS AT B.M.C." (M.E.HARRIS, M.I.T. PRESS) gave us immediate visual recollection, but it was the present voices that made the past present.
MOST OF US WERE STUDENTS FROM THE MIDDLE FORTIES PERIOD.- THE WAR YEARS.- (THE MAILING HAD GONE OUT ONY TO THE NEW ENGLAND STATES) AND OF THE FACULTY ONLY MOLLY GREGORY AND M.C. RICHARDS COULD COME, BUT OTHERS SENT THEIR GREETINGS.
we missed you, and missed many, many faces from other times! There might to be one more reunion for them.- this time on the west coast? it would be worth the effort (even for some of us here to rejoin) because the spirit of B.M.C. is fast slipping from reality to myth.
IF YOU ARE INTERESTED IN HELPING TOWARDS SUCH A GATHERING YOU COULD CONTACT M.E.HARRIS FOR SOME MAILING ADDRESSES (42 GROVE STR./ NEW YORK.N.Y. 10014) AND SPREAD THE WORD?
30 years of living in New York, freelanding as a children's book illustrator among other things, raising a daughter of 2, and (sadly) separating from Charles 20 yrs.ago and later remarrying another architect, and keeping in touch with The Dreiers, has not dimmed the memory of magic B.M.C.!- It would be wonderful to see you again!
