credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Slats, it seems like a couple of aeons ago I received the announcement of your marriage to some Lucian Marquis, last of the Romans.
Oneo f these days I intend to remember this thing with a little substance, but now i'm at th world's end and there are nothing buy palm fans, sandspure, and pine needles here, in boiling sunlight to the small dead business center of town, where there ain't nothing: no book store, no antique shop, not even a respectable fish market where I might buy you a beautiful blue and white crab, remove the raw flesh with a pair of miscroscopic tweezers, and send it for you to wear on your head to the ritziest kind of dives.
As I know very well that you're as luminous as the evening star these days I'm not going to quiz you. Happy, happy Slats. Many honeymoons to you.
Peggy is almost married too. Plan to marry come June 1st, New York, to the Knopf publicity director, on William Cole, who is compounded of light and air, warmth and golden chains, humored with funny language and conceits, 6'1" tall, slender, curleyhaired, happy, at east anywhere, forward, never still, and he loves to eat snails, venison, read James Joyce and Mencken's The American Language, and he spoils me to death. He hates the Catholic church and all formal religions, he loves to take excursions anywhere under the sun, he landed in Europe a little after D Day, loved Paris and went deep into Germany, loves to sing Welsh songs and Schuman songs in a beautiful tenor, stayed in an old caste in Wales for a long time during the war...
This could reel on into the night.
Was at Black Mountain for a while this Spring. The Dreiers are as quietly magnificent as ever, Dehn, and others. But as usual I had to spring back out again after a while. You can see enough of some people, and I saw enough of the Rondthalers to last me many many moons. I was secretary to the registrar.
Well, Adios, and best to you.
Peggy

title: 2 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dear Slats
Hearing from you is better than smelling a bakery. I’ve had acquaintances who wrote friendship to death and usually I dread entering into a correspondence, but I certainly have enjoyed hearing from you.
I’ve read about such places as Osai in THE NEW YORKER (whose thin satire seems about as sterile to me as ice and ash) but your description delighted me much more.
My book will be published Jan.9. Believe me I dread it. I’ve already had the reactions of several members of my family. My big sister says that I’m “frustrated.” My mother cannot understand why I must mention “nastiness.” I’d send you a copy of this terrible book if I hadn’t already given away the 6 free copies allotted me. -And I had to give them to people who will be shocked by them.
It’s not a good novel. I’m not so good you see. But I plunged as deep as I could go in two months- I was desperate for money and living in a kind of abject nursery.
Now I’m back in misery again. It feels familiar and almost good. I think I prefer it. Life is so much more poignant- sharp and warm against the cold wet of wretchedness.
If you ever get hold of it I’d be interested in your reactions- so long as you’d be honest. My sister was honest (and rather cruel). As I wrote it (almost automatically) I was only aware of prayer. The parts of the book my mother objects most to were actually disguised pleas for sex education and healthier treatment of it in the world of children. My mother never talked of sex to me. I had to gleam what I know from strange ways and places- meaning books, talk, and other people’s actions along with my own dumb subdued impulses.
I’m delighted to hear of this Lucian. I wish I knew someone I might love and marry. I’d like to be making a home and rearing some children. Bobby Dreier sent me a most precious photograph of little 3 months old Barbara Beate.
Instead I have to work at writing, usually in pain. And I’ve only the town’s stringent reactions to look forward to.
(I got a letter through my editor from a Betram Bloch- story editor in New York for 20th Century Fox Movie C. He praised the book almost excessively except he thinks it too much sociology- But I don’t know this Betram Bloch. I wish I had the counsel of someone I could trust and believe in). I need a “boy friend” Slats
I love to hear of your work- I’ll be soooo glad when you have enough social power to do more as you feel best. I know that no matter what you have to contend with you are trying to do what you understand to be best.
As for your ever being a failure you’ll never come as close to being one as I eternally am. I am ignorant and it seems a hopeless task to even try to educate myself.
Well Slats, all the best to you * Peggy
That’s how Herbert Weinstock, my editor, signs his notes to me, and I keep wondering if he’s sincere or just business like and clever. See the condition of my nasty mind. Love B

title: Letter typed with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Well, hello! Unexpected pleasure. Don’t you think it’s time we pretend to each other that we’re dead?
I’ll send this to your Wedding Announcement address, if I can grab that away from the mouse.
When my novel appeared in Jan.9, 1946, I was so sad my weight dwindled to 95 at one point. My sister has never forgiven me to this day—why I haven’t been quite able to understand—and the town boiled merrily.
Ted Dreier and Bobbie got me a job as secretary to the registrar at Black Mountain. There exists under there a family of middleclass wonders named Rondthaler. I worked under their supervision and that of doctor Miller’s, sometimes playing hookey and writing on my novel in Bobbie Dreier’s bedroom.
March 2 and 3 the publicity director at Knopf came to see me. I promised to marry him the first day I met him. He stayed with Max Dehn, my dear young Max Dehn. There was snow and high pasture and a collie named Jake who lept around like a wave and drank out of little holes full of water in the stones.
I resigned effective March 30, because I couldn’t live the life of two people, writer and 24 hour duty secretary, and visited my publicity director in New York. This was when LIFE got its photograph. We drove out to Jones Beach in a grand Cadillac to get a Florida landscape. Those seven days were the highest mountains of my life. I flew home in a grand singing state of dreaming.
I returned six weeks later and married him June 3 in City Hall, which has Mecurochrome walls in its chapel. The ceremony lasted less than 5 minutes. Neither of us believes in the formal religions.
We were quite poor, as the publicity director had never believed in saving money, so we hitchhiked to a Welsh town named Remsen for our honeymoon. Willie had spent two years overseas in Wales, France, Luxemburg, and Germany.
I wrote five short stories last summer, had a brief sorjourn in the hospital with an ovarian cyst, and am writing my novel now. A short story will appear shortly in PARTISAN REVIEW and another in HARPER’S BAZAAR. Pearl Kazin, Alfred’s sister, and a photographer named Ronnie Jacquez, both from HARPER’S BAZAAR, were up in these humble filthy diggings over the third avenue El Wednesday taking photographs.
My novel, which has a tendency to grow huge, is, the first hundred pages of it, with my editor. The past week has been rest week for me. I’ve done nothing buy play solitaire with a vague air and listen to music over WQXR. I feel like a beachcomber. I sleep until noon every day. But, oh, how I needed relaxation. I get very tense, as you so well know.
Well, that’s that!
Now you, dear Slats. Is Los Angeles still the dream city? I know the weather must be beautiful and glowing green, but we had a wonderful furry blizzard a short time ago, in which Willie and I wallowed like pigs. One first night at one-thirty we went for a long walk in isolated Central Park, so beautiful, the zoo so silent, only the moose and buffalo and foxes with wet beady eyes! The big thoroughfares looked like country lanes. New York was never so beautiful before!
Write me news!
Love Peggy
Miss. William Cole
1025 third avenue
New York City

title: 2 page typed letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dear Slatz:
I just received your letter, and it leaves me with such mixed and truly poignant feelings that I must sit down and answer you immediately-- I've only three weeks of classes left, and they will doubtless be too hectic for any sort of correspondence. And anyway, even tho its very impractical, lteter should be answered while the first feeling of "response" is still true.
What your letter called up in me was a rather dismaying realization of the aptness of a certain metaphor I once came across in a course on Virginia Woolf. It was something to do with her book "the Years"-- which I have just finished and found to be only a little less satisfying than The Lighthouse, which simply floored me. The Years is a story of the lives of one generation of an upper middle-class English family-- something like ten young people, cousins, brothers and sisters etc. The book takes them in a rather strange, unreal narrative from about 1880 up to the present and-- the never openly until the last few pages-- deals with their gradual and inevitable estrangement, their sad but neccessary isolation as human beings. The last scene is a rather ghastly affair of a family reunion-- some have returned from service in India old men, some have grown obese and smug, one has become a social worker, another "Lady so and so" etc., and they fail utterly to communicate or find a common denominator of interest or sympathy. Well! to get back to that far off metaphor. It was one of a wheel. Their youthful community spokes-- but without a rim. Quite a fine image, I thought, a wheel without a rim, and could immediately see its general truth, but I somehow never thought of its applying to people who were "real" friends-- theose liveswere parallel or intertwined or cross-crossing. Well your letter called up the wheel-- veddy depressing thought, no? It was quite formal in an odd sort of way I can't quite put my finger on. You are even more on the defensive now about BMC than you were when you wrote me from there in January-- a fact about which I can conjecture, but won't know much about until I talk to you sometime. One of the reasons I'm sorry to know I won't see you for a long time now is that too much time between the BMC issue and the time when you and I will probably evaluate it again will probably tend to obscure the problems and, on the surface, lessen their importance. You once wrote words to the effect that you realized, now, that I had been right about a number of things, a statement i admired and for which I was really grateful. I must admit that I two was wrong in certain ways, but in making, or rather failing to make, certain distinctions, and being too prone to generalizations, bothin my allegiances and in my condemnations. Well, someday, we will tell each other what we really mean, but enough of this rather somber meandering for now.
I know you will be happy to hear, if you haven't already, that Anatole is in the US now. Actually he's at Walter Reed hospital in Washington DC, but he's very well and comes to New York whenever he can get away. I was at the Kopps on Saturday night and it was wonderful to see him.
I, of course, was properly impressed by your decision to paint seriously, and feel absolutely cheated that I didn't get to see your exhibition etc. Really, what an appaling lack of imagination I have! I was actually very anxious to get in touch with you During March, you know--cheer you on, hear how things were progressing, etc.. but did it once enter my mind that I could call you on the phone? Most certainly not, so I sat silently gnashing my teeth when Liese and Janie told me how they had done so. Not only that but I sent you an entreaty for news on a lovely Matisse postcard. Of course, I didn't put any address on the card, but I did write a nice long message and even put on a three-cent stamp. Disintegration!
My life is generally quite dull except for my class with Sidney Hook and the occassional times I spend with Martine. Haven't I written you since I've been living with the Howard Fasts? They are extremely depressingand exasperating people to live with, although they mean very well. But they are, I discovered to my dismay, two of the most dogmatic and ignorant of all communists I even hope to meet: real fanatics, and, to me, fanatics are the most evil people in the world.
But Martine is charming-- I haven't words enough to praise her "esthetic sensibility" if I may put it that way. She is mainly interested in esthetics, not only in her sculpture, which is very very promising, I think, but in all art forms. She is the most articulate and discerning critic of anyone our age I've ever known. She is going to France in five or six weeks and is exceedingly happy about it. You realize, of course, that you and even I have command appearances to make in France after the war-- accordning to both the Kopps and Martine. It seems we work our way over by shepherding children on a liner.
Speaking selfishly, I hope you decide against going to Mexico. But a summer with your sister sounds very exciting. I think Kenton will be good also-- John Crowe Ransom will give a class which I can take since I'll only be working part-time. Eric and Maja will probaby be there for a few weeks, and I think Fritz intends to ask Barzun to come and lecture, but I doubt that we'll be successful. After that, I'm flat broke and haven't the vaguest idea what to do wit my life. One encouraging but extremely ephemeral (?) light on the horizon is that Hook liked a review of Harold Laski's last book that I wrote for him so much, that he is showing it to the editors of the Partisan Review-- (much hysterical laughter, pliz). So maybe I could dupe some sort of publication into giving me a job sweeping up the office or something. Ahr well, leave us not think on such grim subjects. What I really want to be is a dilletante. (Hold your fire, friend) Oh, you asked about my graduation. Well, Im all finished except for a 6 point requirement in classics which I must make up, God knows when. I wanted to take a class with Barzunat Columbia next year if possible, but I've just learned that he now has a Guggenheim fellowship and plans to take off a year to write a book on Hector Belioz. Woe is me. Eric has a wonderful deal from Minnesota for next year ist seems. The U. of Chicago (of all places) offered him a much better paying position, but Minnesota was so anxious to keep him that they gave him an Assistant Professorship and a special schedule of only 7 hours a week of classes'. Isn't it disgusting- but really very swell for him. Also he has recently become one of the editors of the Kenyon Review.
Well Slats, it was very very good to hear from you, and I'm exceedingly disappointed that you aren't coming to New York. There's really no need to repeat how mutual the fondness you speak of is. If I thought on it long, I'm sure I could weep real tears. beeg fat ones, over the difference in our relationship last spring and this. Gee, I have Black Mountain-sickness this eve. I'm late for seeing a performance of Hamlet with Martine now, so I'll stop drooling. Please write again soon-- we ought to puta rim on at least two of the spokes, n'est pas? Much love Jeanne

title: 2 page typed with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
237 West 11th St.
May 30, 1955
Dearest Slats:
I'm sure everyone will be more comfortable if I don't try to explain why I was such a wretch about answering your delightful telegram or your Christmas card. Actually the card came into my hands in February, and since about that time it has seemed to me pointless to communicate with anyone until I could share some good news. Obviously a very subjective attitude, but for the last few months I've been in the final throes of my dissertation, and couldn't bear to say "It's just about finished" to anyone, especially in writing! So anyway, it's finished, and I can begin to behave like a human being again. How ARE you, my dear Slats and Lucien and Josh? And what in the World are you doing in OREGON? I know I don't deserve an answer, but thank you our friends don't treat us according to our desers, so I shall expect a great fat letter- sometime!
Shall I try to catch you up? Maybe it's enough to say that shortly after Tom and I were married and moved here, I settled down to a serious try at my dissertation, hoping to submit it in April '54. Obviously, I didn't make it, and it hung horridly over me for the whole damn year. Besides which we had to do all sorts of major paint and construction jobs on this apartment last summer. During the winter I taught one course at NYU and worked two days a week for Spanish Refugee Aid (helping Republican refugees in the south of France), and, by dint of lord knows what effort, get the thesis into shape. Tom has been teaching a freshman English course at Pratt Institute and working for the Reading Laboratory part-time, and was away in England for 7 weeks for the latter. Oh dear! such boring statistics on how we earn our bread! I just tried to find you a snapshot of us and can't. How annoying! Because you can tell from Tom's face that he is terribly nice, and its probably bad taste for me to elaborate in that vein. I begin to despair of your ever having an opportunity to see for yourself. But a year from now we may make a big effort to find teaching jobs in the West, and then, maybe......
Blake Ehrlich was asking about you both last week. Denny (alias Ginger) brought their bouncing son Luke back to the US last summer to display some to grandparents and Blake finally arrived in February. He's just gone back and she will follow shortly. He's been doing pretty well as a freelancer in Europe, and I fear they've become real expatriates, which I disapprove of, for no very rational reason. (I mean my disapproval isn't very rational, not their preferences.) Actually, Tom and I are pining to go back to Europe together for a year, and may make it two years from now, if thinks work out as we plan. What ever happened to your yern to go to Japan? For all I know, you may have gone and returned already! Isn't it shameless that I can admit such a possibility, that I've been out of touch for so long? I thought of you in that connection last week when Andy and I were caught in a lovely thunderstorm in the Japanese exhibition house in Red Hook, NY (near Bard College, Poughkeepsie, etc.) Fred commutes to Columbia, spending three nights in the City nd four in the country, and Andy gardens, battles the termites, has innumerable weekend guests and seems generally to be enjoying life hugely. Whom else can I tell you about? I saw Albers' show this winter and liked some canvases very well- the ones with big, simple blocks of saturated colors, wonderful colors.
You are probably up on the news about Janie and Fred Stone better than I, but in case not, I heard from Blake that they have three children and may be in for a fourth, and that Fred makes many photographs for money and Janie bakes her own bread. My Arlyn and Mark Brunswick have finally separated, but she is quite ill, psychologically and with hepatitis, and Mark seems to be the only one to take care of her. It is a terribly sad and muddled business. Addison Bray seems to be turning into a confirmed bachelor, as they say; working at night and writing in the day and drifting in and out of my orbit about every six months. And that is all the news of BMC I can scare up at the moment, except that Ruth Miller dances in Jose Limon's troup and seems to be very good at it.
I'm looking forward to next winter in NY-- at least it will be one year when I can spend some time enjoying this dirty and fascinating place without constant deadlines of an academic nature! I'll be teaching one course at NYU and perhaps two, but I'm getting quite used to teaching and don't spend half my life in preparation, as I used to. I'll take piano lessons again and probably drive poor Tom to drink with practiving. I'm also supposed to think about working my dissertation into English, and a book, but that's a long project, and at this point I have no stomach even to contemplate it. If Lucien finished his (I actually don't know) he'll understand my present mood, I'm sure. Tom and I both have vague plans to finish our respective courses (or is it opi?) on that projected visit to Europe, but the less said the better.
What a miserable show at a letter! There is only one solution. How about coming to Albequerque (it's less than halfway!) next month while I'm visiting my mother? I do think that would be an excellent plan. Or go to visit your mother in Ogden, and we could meet halfway- at Pikes Peak or something? If you have any other ideas, out with them! Do you know Slats, it's been five years! It isn't fair. We should all be rich and spend summers at watering places together, at least.
Write me soon, so I can cope with this awful nostalgia. And send me a snap of your son if you remember. I wouldn't mind a bit if you were in it too! But, best of all, tell me what you're doing and planning and enjoying.
Much love greetings from Tom Jeanne

title: 7 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dearest ole Slatz!
How nice to hear from you! Seems impossible that it was two whole years ago that we sat on the dam- on my birthday I remember- and argued with tears streaming down our faces because it hurt so much to have the other one on the opposite side; and because it was a schism that no logical or argumentative acrobatics could bridge. Tho at the time I could conceive of anothing more painful and tragic, when I think back now it appears quite a beautiful and priceless experience to have had such a friendship.
What torture it was to argue with you and get how (?) "wrong" it seemed for us not to be in agreement. But even tho I can see now how unphilosophic and irrational my attitude was. I'm really glad I had it. At last I'm beginning to lose my very dogmatic bias against "irarational" behavior and to enjoy some experiences that are valuable precisely because they are more human and instinctual than they are efficient and rational. My goodness! I don't really know whether this small torrent of reflection is due to my having just this moment finished reading Santoyana's "The Realm of Truth" or because the very philosophic young man sitting in a chair across the room has had quite a profound effect on my thinking during the past few weeks since I (obstensibly) married him.
(It looks equally fantastic from where I stand every now and then, dear Slats, so don't be too amazed at this news.) Shall I write you pages and pages about him? I could, but I know it aint polite. He is just horribly intelligent and sensitive and has the most unbiased creative and truly philosophical mind I have ever seen in a person less then 40 years old- and he's only 22, a year younger than myself. To give you a vague idea- he's been a sincere practitioner of yoga, had mystic experiences, was for two years a rabid and active communist, has tremendously catholic abilities ranging from golf and chess to symbolic logic, and is humorous, and kind and lovable on top of it all. Really you must excuse all this rhetoric- you are the first person I've had to write about this, and I'm a little over-exhuberant I guess. He was raised in South America and we hope to send the next year in Brazil with his parents for various and sundry reasons, and then both return and go to Graduate School. He wants to teach and write- philosophy mainly- and I hope to make a few feeble efforts in the same direction. Our interests are very similar, except that his are broader than mine at the moment, but I'm becoming less of a provincial every day- at necessity, or I get teased to death. I had to give up my scholarship at NYU, but I hope that Hook can wrangle me one for the following year. Of course, Eva and my mother had to bangle things up as completely as possible by rushing to NY as soon as R wrote them about it. It was really comic- poor Don and I, in the midst of final examinations, not knowing each other too well, packing for Canada and Brazil, not having time to get married before the family-ogre arrrived, but determined not to do it with them around. I lost ten pounds and developed a few twitches, but am fat and happy again here on this nice farm on Prince Ed. Island. We do nothing but read and eat and swim- and paint (me) and shall probably be here until Don's parents arrive from S.A. at the end of July.
Well, dahlinh, I hope this isn't so incoherrent that you can't see how happy I am. Now I must tell you the rest of the news. Andy- whether as a result of contagen or not, I can't tell- just married her very very nice Literature professor at Bard- Fred Dupree- about two weeks ago. I only saw her for a few minutes the day I left for Canada and she came to NY from Bard, and of course she was vague and non-committal about it then, but Aryln wrote me that it was true a few days ago. Gawd! Enough of this society-page news!
I've been so damn envious about you. Paul Radin was in NY a few weeks ago and told Arlyn about Varda's going to Black Mountain, and I thought I detected your influence lurking around somewhere. Your letter sounded depressed and the people at Tahoe sound horrid. What did you mean about the business of selling out being insurrmountable? What have you been doing since Christmas? Painting like a "painter" only not in the garret? Please write me what are your plans, if any, Speaking of New York, I still have my apartment at 181 Thompson. Addison Bray is renting it for the summer, but I haven't made any arrangement with him for the fall- it is completely finished, even with my books, so that if you do plan to come to NY soon enough, you might want to live there, yes? Know hwo is in N.Y. again?  Big Swack- he takes piano lessons just across the street from the Cohens' place and they see him now and then. I haven't seen him, but Arlyn saw both him and Sam Brown at a concert at Columbia a few weeks ago. Do you ever hear from him? Excuse the prying, but I was away when he last came to BMC, and after I got back you and I were on such queer terms that I never dared ask you what had happened.
Eric and Maja were supposed to be in NY a couple of weeks after and left- his book is just out and he is busily writing another on GB Shaw for New Direction's Matter of Mod.Lit.series. I haven't written them since about March, so I don't know what goes on there.
Ginger Osbourne is trying to break into the modelling business and is doing quite well, I think. She gets more beautiful every time I see her.
Are you interested in all this chatter? It all seems very far away to me at the moment, and probably more so to you. But California sounds so lonely- why don't you think seriously about NY for a change? Isn't it horrible that you when you might get to the beeg city, I leave? I would so like you to knoe Don- I have talked about you to him and we agree that you are our favorite delectable mountain. He would amuse you I'm sure- tall and thin and grey and professional- looking already; terribly proper to all surface appearance, but with the most absolutely unconventional soul I've ever known. I'm off again, and it's all so useless since letters, as you observed, are completely inadequate. But please write me again soon and tell me what you think about life and all such other more juicy questions. What you have been painting or learning or deciding, etc.
Don't let Tahoe get you down.
Lotz of loff
Jeanne
Jeanne Hodges
c/o Mac Millan
Fairview
Prince Edward Island
Canada

title: 3 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
4/21/46
Darling ole Slatz-
I wrote you a long, exuberant and quite unintelligible letter about six weeks ago- and never mailed it because I had enclosed a copy of the BARD Review and didn't know what the postage would be without a trek to the U.S. Post Office. So don't think I've forgotten thee.
Where are you- you great big delectable mountain? Are you in San Francisco? Your last letter December I think- sounded as tho you might well end up in Tahiti or some god-forsaken spot just to escape all the complications. WRITE TO ME OR I SHALL SET ON THE BLOODHOUNDS!!!
Christ! It's been months! I can't think where to begin- I just want to communicate. By the way, I finally found the issue of Circle with the article on Varda. He sounds extremely interesting- but I do wish Miller hasn't been so damn coy about it all.
As for me, I'm in a terribly chastened and humble mood. So many nice things have happened to me, and I feel like a big fake because of it. Oh- the Bard Review- it's a wonderful idea which will probably fold up after the next issue. Published by a bunch of students at Bard- Andy, Addison, Kitty, Molly, etc.- you'll see the names on the editorial board. Anyhoo, being desperate for material they used an article of mine- so I am published! which is very funny! If I can snatch a copy back from Arlyn I'll send it. Also- I have a scholarship to get an M.A. in philosophy next year at NYU- which is also funny, since it was all due to Sidney Hook's machinations on my behalf- talk about a guardian angel! Oh- Andy and I were introduced to high "lit'ry society" last weekend. Her teacher, F.W. Dupree, who used to be an editor at Parisan Review and who, I am sure, is completely fascinated by Andy, took us to the annual P.R. cocktail party where we sat qualing and gaping and meeting all sort of horribly famous people. It was very deflating and we both decided to retire to a nunnery in the near future.
What are you going to do in the summer? We plan to make boards of money by being waitresses at some summer resort- so that I, at least, can go to school next year without working. I have a rather good job at the moment- doing research and reading for Bantam Books- a new 25-c Reprint publisher. Will Hamlin is their main render and got me the job.
I saw Marita Pevsner yesterday for the first time since BMC- and Ginger Osbourne is on the verge of becoming a veddy successful model for Harper's etc. She looks wonderful. Arlyn lives on Washington Square just a couple of blocks from the me and I'm afraid is turning into a dilettante doll-wife. Damn Mark Brunswick! Does all this gossip interest you? Probably not, but I had such a session of it yesterday that it's still running out of my ears.
My new idol is James Burnham who is teaching an excellent aesthetics class and who is probably the most perceptive and intelligent person I've ever seen. I'm in the midst of a ghastly paper on IH Richards for him right now, so this letter is really the result of procrastination. I'm also taking a class in Scientific Method from him- and you'd be amused to see me wrestling with Einstein's General Theory of Relativity! It sounds impressive, but believe me, I'm a babe in the woods.
Slatz I really must stop. Can't possibly say half of what I want to anyway. But pliz pliz write immediately. I simply refuse to lose contact with thee. My best love and a pox on you if I don't hear from you by return mail.
Jeanne

title: Handwritten letter on notebook paper with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dearest friend Slats-
So! another indian bit the dust! I was highly suprised and delighted- altho all I remember of Lucian is a large smile and dark hair. Please let me wish you all the pssible nice wonderful and joyous things to be wished on such a momentuous occasion!
And please forgive my stunned silence- after all, it isn't every day that one's very favorite delectable mountain announces her marriage and I was anticipating the promised letter. (I pause to glower- is that a word?- in your direction.)
Please regard this note as a large club or a gadfly or something suitable to make your leap into action with pen in hand- please!
I've begun to regard California as sort of a Circus island from which you will never return now. Anyway, both of us are nursing the desire to the similarity enchanted, and there's a real posability that we may submt as soon as we've pocketed our degrees. "Quail Drive" sounds almost pastoral from here.
Are you quite serious about the convenience of our arriving there one day this summer? We are counting the weeks till Utah and California can't be too unreasonably far, as I recall.
Even tho my own delight in this whole affair is quite irrelevant to it's "essence." I respect that I think it wonderful!
Be charitable in the form of a long letter, dear Slats.
lof Jeanne

title: Letter typed with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dear OleZlats:
First let me assure you that the letter was mailed-- a couple of days later, I'm afraid, cause I was more or less flat on my back with my old "complaint" when your letter arrived. Such excitement! I want to TALK to you! Heep happy--listen to me worry; Just in case--which I really don't expect-- you do decide to come to NY. I can't offer you a bed until February, since Andy will be staying here until then. Th Bard College kids have a "work period" of six or seven weeks. However!
Point number two: Anatole and Marrianne are leaving for France! on the 20th of December-- they are very sad about not seeing you-- and are having a sort of BMC get-together next sunday to say Farewell. This is related to the bed problem because Mme. Kopp isn''t going with them, and will have lots of room and would be delighted to have you stay there I'm sure. Oh, what the hell! We will sling a hammock-- there is lots of room once you get here--if you do.
My life (sex) has developed complications too, but this is no place to go into said mess.Oh, to be neuter gender--as Andy and I have often observed in our back-to-the-womb moments.
Of course New York is the "be all and the end all."!! Just come and see. I saw "Androcies and the Lion" last night-- a veddy baaaad producation by the New School's dramatic workshop-- but even they couldn't entirely spoil Shaw's dialogue.
Oh dear, Slats, I used to scoff at people who said they were too busy "living" to study and read books, but I'm becoming more sympathetic ot their point of view. It takes an amount of discipline that is simply appalling! I think I'm just damn sick of having to support myself and try to study at the same time...just the physical problem of time, and keeping clean, and "seeing people" becomes too much for me, at times. Pardon my griping.
So. you're rediscovering Donne. I'm rediscovering Yeats. Remember "Sailing to Byzantium" which Eric made you analyse once? I had to do the same thing for Branham's Aesthetics class, and am practically inarticulate with awe and admiration. I think I must have read that poem two dozen times before, and never understood it until now. But what keeps going through my head tonight is that crazy line from Dover Beach-- something about "the world, which seems to lie before us like a land of dreams, so various, so beautiful, so new..." And I haven't ben drinking. The other Yeats poem which has knocked me out this week you may have forgotten or may not know, so I shall quote it to you in its entirety (ahem) and then stop this drivel.
Speech, after long silence. It is right,
All other lovers being estranged or dead,
Unfriendly lamplight hid beneath my shade,
The curtains drawn against unfriendly night,
That we should now discant, and yet again discant
Upon the supreme theme of Art and Song.
Bodily decrepitude is wisdome; Young
We loved each other and were ignorant.
What a weird letter....I think I ought to have been drinking.
Write me again, pliz, and let me know how your "buyer" is making out in her attempt to make you a beeg success.
luv Jeanne

title: 5 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
August 28
Dearest Slate-
I guess this second day of my bedridden state is just the time to answer your good long letter. (No, i'ts not a baby-just bronchitis, as usual.) Of course, I'm most curious to hear whether ort any of the vrious and sundry possibilities for a job turned out to be fruitful. I certainly hope so. So write me all about it- what ever became of the lady with leopard-skin slacks, surrounded by Klees? Gee, most of them sound like part of the lunatic fringe, but it must be quite enlightening to meet them face to face- and in their natural habitat, so tp speak.
I have been spending a rather lazy summer- a result of circumstances in part, and in part a result of my own lack of discipline. The Aesthetics course from John Crowe Ransom was a disappointment to be the Rudy and me. (she is here for the summer, too. Plans to graduate from Bard College next June in Literature under F.W. Dupree (poetry.ed of the nation) and to write her senior project on Kafka.) ransom may be a fine poet, but as a teacher of philosophy he is impossible. He is terribly gentle and polite- the southern gentleman, per excellence. But he never defines a term, and loves to expound his own theory of art as expiation endlessly. It is a very interesting and highly fruitful theory. I think mainly Freudian- although it took two or three weeks at vague lectures for us even to make this connection thank gawd Eric is here to do some interpreting. But I think that Aesthetics is probably the most ill defined and unexplored of all philisophic studies. Anyways, it's just been rather frustrating to me. The Cultural Hiistory of the Ren. has been a nice, dillatantish pastime, taught by extremely sophisticated German scholar named Salomon. Other than this, I've managed to read finally th Magic Mountain and Moby Dick, which latter is probably my favorite novel to date and to attend innumerable concerts, reciatls, etc. Erie just gave a very provocative lecture on "Are the Muses Really Sisters?" in which he discussed the problems of the ersate culture which has arisen since it was discovered that it could be a commodity and the object  at mass production. He has just finished his bookk on the drama which should come out early next year, I guess.
Speaking of books, it seems I have myself a completely weird job editing one for Evich Leinsdouf, conductor of the Cleveland Symphony Orch. He was here to give a lecture and I did a little re-writing for him then, and he suddenly had an intuitive insight to the effect that I was just the person who could do this book for him. It's really a snap of a job, if all goes well and I'm capable of it. He will be in Cleveland, and I will be in New York working at my own convenience for 1.50 per hour. I haven't the vaguest idea what shape the manuscript is in or anything, but I think its a good opportunity to do something concrete at least. I can also finish my six-point requirement at NYU at the same time, so I guess my life a generally organized for the fall, at least.
I'm rather terrified about it, nonetheless. Andy will be at Bardi Fran has a position at a ritzy girls' college in upper New York called Wells; Arlyn is married to Mark Brunswick and they don't know where they'll be; Martine Seligman has gone to France, in other words, I'm probably going to be lonely as can be- maybe I'll get some solid reading done then, tho. (Don't laugh, but I nt to read Greek + Roman History and Philosophy on my own next year) I'm so thoroughly ignorant at both.) Arn't you ever coming to New York? What in the wold has the west coast got? I know, Gram and Helen ahd Vicki sound wonderful, but after all, New York is New York etc.
I guess I won't get home to see my family this summer, which is another rather shocking break with tradition for them. It's funny, when I'm sick I think about them a lot, as I have the last couple of days, but otherwise, I hardly remember them. No roots, no roots! I'm feeling quite disintegrated at this point. One contributing factor is the spectacle of Arlyn's marriage. I don't want to seem a shrew, but I don't think it was a good idea, and I don't think it will last at all. Mark brings out all of her light-headed and undisciplined qualities and does nothing at all to encourage her to work or study. He is a terribly spoiled child and a dilletante, to boot. Gee, I think there is nothing that gives me the creeps more than someone who is perpectually bored! Ernst Krenek, (he's here again this summer) is the classic case, but Mark is one, too. Dr. Jalo was here for a couple of weeks, and I heard a really terrifying conversation between him and Ransom about the fact that even the very young people were bored and sorted now, before they had really experienced anything. Of course, one had always heard this about the "fin de siecle" in general, but I had somehow never included myself. Now I begin to wonder. Is the reason that I don't know "what I want to do" that I've not discovered where my hypothetical talents lie, just that I'm unable to get enthusiastic over anything? I've always thought myself a very enthusiastic person, but maybe that's only passive enthusiasm which doesn't demand action and produce results. Ah well, pardon the slight figuring of the personality. Anyhoo, Ransom thinks it's because living nowadays is so easy. We seldom come up against anything that really taxes our ingenuity or resourcefullness, and therefore we feel we know it all. I guess he's still somewhat tof an Agrevian. Eric and Maja gave me a copy of his new book of selected poems, but although I've read them twice, I certainly don't think I got most of them. Do you still write poetry in your odd moments?
Gee, Slate, how nice it would be to see you and take to you again! I am much much less bitter about BMC now, I think. In fact, I seldom think about any of its unpleasant memories anymore. Did you, by the way, see Eric's article on Black Mountain in the summer Partisan Reiew. I know that I did, and perhaps you will, find it remarkably objective, straightforward and fair. He comes to a rather pesimistic conclusion about experimental colleges in general, but it's by no means a startling conclusion- a number of us had come to that conclusion tentatively last summer. Not that I myself, knowing what I know, wouldn't go to BMC if I had the chance to make over again; but even so, I'm inclined to think that the ills that we suffered there are more ot less inherent in the whole set up, so that I don't think it would be a good place to stay for four years. (Don't know what I'm getting so pompous about.)
Didn't I ever write you about my so-called new political development? I'm sure I did. Maybe your exclamation of curiosity was just an exclamation and not a request for more details. Gawd! I think that intellectual indeguity is the most impossible of all virtues to attain! The others are mere childs-play- tho I suppose its the some with what one might call artistic opinions and (?) of a group- any group, and to cease thinking things through for yourself- to decide at one time that the socialists are right or the communistts, or the republicans and then to assume that they will always be right in the future, too. But it's such a pleasant state to be in- to have a group which believes as you do, and it must be almost impossibly difficult to renounce such a comfort.
Fritz Cohen was just in to see me. Now everyone is off to hear Kolla Graudan play the unaccompanied cello suites by Bach, and the campus  is wonderfully peaceful. But Fritz and Andy send you their best regards. Please, Slatz dear, let me hear from you again soon, and I shall have something besides convalescent drivel to tell you. Many things must have happened to you in this month and a half. By the way, have you read Moby Dick and did you find it completely wonderful as I did? He really wrote- with American English. I also read out of her shorter novels, but I don't think it has anything of the genius in Moby DIck.
I'll leave a forwarding address here, just in case you don't write soon- but please do.
Moch loff Jeanne
P.S. Did anything happen about your fascinating Mr. Eames?

title: 2 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Dearest Slats-
I'm reading "the Enormous Room" after lo these many years, and at last grasping the essence of a fine concept which I'm sure you introduced me to- that of Delectable Mountains! So all things- guilt, found memoirs, E.E. Cummings, foul weather- conspire to produce this shamefully overdue communication. I am as you see from the address, sojourning till the end of June at this curious estate- which you probably know about from one source or another. A fine robber baron and his eccentric wife left their estate and a wad of money to the devoted- and I quote- to the advancement of the arts and letters. Which menas that artists and writers are invited to spend a month or two here during the summer, working. We are splendidly housed and fed and all but washed and combed, while here, and guaranteed utter quiet and privacy. I'm here under the guise of "writer", since I'm embarked on another PhD. dissertation- this time it's do or die, since my venture into the non-academic world last spring convinced me that the Groves of Academe were a million times preferable to the jungle of New York offices. So I spent last winter working half-day to keep body and soul joined, and passing German and other exams for a Ph.D. Now, I'm on that last and roughest lap- as Lucian will doubtless agree- trying to write a dissertation- in Aesthetics yet! If I'm clever, I'll take a long winter for a fellowship which may get me to Europe next summer. I went down to New York a few days ago to see Anoly and Fred Dupree and their two kidlets off on the Sole de France, (They're going to spend a year or more in France and Italy), and the excursion left me helecious with envy and nostalgia. Are you and Lucian pining and planning to go back? How goes Lucian's dissertation? Since I naturally misplaced your last-summer's letter, I recall only that he was working at it and that you were meriting money from the movie monguls, teaching their distrubed children to paint. So fo please bring me up to date! My excuse is really, I suppose, that I have had nothing world-shaking or even especially happy to report on my doings, coping with lonliness and relative poverty circumstances. Yadds is a fairly pleasant respute, although, as you can imagine, a collection of twenty or so "creative" souls is not thte most harmonious circle conceivable.
As forr news of mutual friends, there really isn't too much. Marita Pevsner was in New York this winter- and promptly got married. I see Arlyn Burnswich and Addison Bray now and then, and Andy quite often. Fritz and Elsa Cohen are as lovely and delightful as ever. Noah Greenberg is divorced from his wife, and I still study piano with him and sing in his madrigal group. You'd be amused to hear, probably, that a boy named Brossand wrote what was intended to be an utterly damning novel about my old friend Anatole, but failed immensibly to plumb the depths of his peculiar hand of destructiveness. It's a bad book, but gave a fairly accurate account of Village lige as she is (?) by some, in case you're curious. Incidentally, I read at the same time a really splendid new novel. Ralph Ellison's "Invisible Man" which everyone should treat himself to. It carries such an imaginative walley and is so wildly and beautifully written that it would be useless to try to convey of its quality in a letter. See for yourselves is my most humble advice!
Merde! What dreadful death dealing old mousters Time Distance are! And what ridiculous weapons, letters. Aren't you ever going to get within hauling distance of New York again? Or how about New Mexico next month? Do you ever drive to Ogden, and if so, Alburquerque is a mere bagatelle on the way. Anyway, its nice to think that we might all get together again before we're sixty! You have my permission to ignore this last flight and simply write me what you're currently planning, thinking, doing, etc. T'would be so nice- especially here at Yaddo,, so I could foil the "Moping Room", which, for your information, is situated right next to meal table and is excusably graced glumly by a dozen or so of us inmates around mail time. Anyway, have a beautiful delectable summer- and WRITE!
LOVE TO YOU AND YOU Jeanne

title: Handwritten letter with envelope

description:
SUNDAY
SLATS-
My darling- this is so wonderful!!!
I’m just as happy as I can be- I love you and want you to live happily ever after.
But you know this spoils all my plans… I was looking around just now for an airplane coming to CALIFORNIA to drop out of the skies and marry you myself.
But such is the tragic life…
By the way- isn’t that name familiar, LUCIAN MARQUIS?
Tell me about him- I’d like to see the man who added more stars to your eyes. I bless you- with my love, Dick WIKE- my tragic life- wasting time on the things these people think important. Pres. of honorary architectural fiat… Pres. Of religious group (Presbyterian)… In the midst of campus-wide election….
Give anything for a few nights at BLACK MTN!... polkas, those wiggly pictures- VALENTINES!

title: 5 page handwritten letter with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
MONDAY
SLATS-
Your letter of last APRIL was beautiful and inspiring- whenever I read it over I want so much to jump into an airplane and come flying out to UTAH or CALIFORNIA or MEJICO… but I haven’t and probably won’t- I’m too dammed practical…
I’m more proud of you than you’d ever guess for showing that you have the real heart of an ARTIST… BMC will somebody come to be just as proud of you as I am now- but by then I’ll be so proud of you that I’ll probably antagonize all of my friends by boasting that I know JANE SLATER…
Now tell me what you’ve been doing… Sean GREG AIN? Been to MEJICO? Earn lots of money? Paint lots of pictures? You haven’t found any young man to take the place of your art have you? I am interested in just whatever you may want to tell me.
As for myself- since last wrote I’ve done some flying getting as far west as DENVER but never having the opportunity to get to either OGDEN or LOS ANGELES…
I was flying the 4 engine LIBERATORS when the end of the war cancelled the demand for eager young men so I was fortunate enough to get out as a surplus pilot…
That little matter of SEPARATION put me home as a civilian on 19.DEC. just in time for CHRISTMAS at home. That takes care of all the details and you are now right up to date on me as all I’ve done since then is get back into the UNIVERSITY OF FLORIDA under the G.I. BILL so that Uncle Sugar pays now instead of Dick Wyke…
From Albers I have a letter- he says they have 73 students. Half a dozen are graduate art students- FOSTER is back- FORBERG, PAGE, and STOLLER are at HARVARD architecture school… CLAUDE  and NAN are about to get married.
And the most unhappy news- DR. JALOWETZ died suddenly from an heart attack following a SATURDAY night concert… that is a great loss, a terrible thing..
SLATS, I want to know everything about you now so I hope you can find time to write a letter someday soon…
Don’t you think he’s HANDSOME?
SLATS I’ll be waiting to hear from you some time soon…
Much, much love, Dick

title: Letter typed with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Slatso fatso,
Just last night, after having finally returned to N.Y., the Stollers came to grace our dinner table and again I am weak with weeping and my heart is bleeding and my face is a nasty shade of green. I don’t think I’ll ever forgive myself or Armando for not having had a part in that journey. God, every picture is a stage set, and the life you must have led seems, from my vantage point of New York’s dreary and drudgery, like the land of the lotus eaters and the elysian fields rapped up in one shiny package. What seems even more depressing is the fact that both you and the Stollers are so far away even now, and there is just no one left in this depressing city who can add a dash of herbs salvia. Nanna looks plumply pregnant and maternal, which becomes her very well. They’re probably going to live on some vast estate near Boston which belongs to the in-laws of Rudy Haase and they have extended us the warmest invitation. But since we are carless for the present we probably won’t be able to take advantage of this for quite a while. I understand that Mimi and her husband have gone to Florida (how permanently I don’t know) and Bob Blisses are in Europe. Even so there is lots of good company there, so that even Boston seems a far, far better place to be than G.D.D.D.D.N.Y. (short for God Damn Dreary Drab New York). As for California- what the h- are you complaining about! It may not be ImO. (meaning Italy, first and foremost) but it is sunny and warm and you are there and that puts it already on quite a different plane.
Now that I’ve bitched enough I’ll describe some of the less drum aspects of our humdrum existence. The Davenports, Lanou and Patsy, have gotten us into a group singing modern music which has been meeting every couple of weeks. Armando only listens so far, but I have hopes of getting him to sing too. Then we also get together for recorder playing once in a while which takes care of our musical needs. We went to see the Horse Show which, except for the horses, was dull and diamond-studded. Most often we go to the movies (strenuously avoiding anything sad or problematical) and occasionally to the theater or opera. The apartment still takes up the greatest part of our time and money. As you know they’ve been building in it since the middle of the summer and everything is still in an unholy mess. The only room which is complete so far is the kitchen, and that is really something to make you happy. Very small and compact and so light you could paint wonderfully there. The wall cabinet (designed by me- Claud says he’ll steel it) has angled walls so that the top shelf is twice the size of the lowest one. The doors slide on ball bearings- very well if noisily. The advantage of such a cabinet is the fact that I preserve all the needed counter space and still have big shelves for the large dishes and platters on top where space is no longer a problem. The walls are covered with grey linoleum in a tile pattern which was cheap, light and easily cleaned. There is a sink, the first I’ve had since I started to cook and a collapsible table, courtesy of Armando, which is very small but holds enough plates for non-company dinners. The ceiling is one large skylight since the room used to be a light shaft, and though a bit drafty it gives the added space and light that completely take away the sense of being cramped such a small room would ordinarily have. Now that the wall between two rooms has been torn down we have an enormous and beautifully proportioned living room which still lacks a rug, bookcases, four dining chairs and PICTURES! AND I HOPE YOU KNOW WHAT I’M HINTING AT! We bought an Eames table on sale which is quite beautiful in walnut with steel legs that are collapsible. But getting chairs for this is a big problem which we hope to solve by sending for some reedbottomed ones from Italy. Mrs. Dal Molin promised to send us a furniture catalogue. They do sell some of these chairs here but for such exorbitant sums od money that it’s completely ridiculous. Then a wall was torn down between our old living room unit which is still very much in a state of becoming. The old bedroom is going to be our guest and eventually nursery room. Speaking of guests, we’re very disappointed because they are refusing Armando’s mother a visitors visa because, being eligible for an immigration visa, they are afraid that she’ll come here for good. We had hoped so much to have her here for Christmas, but now it seems easier to get the regular visa which will of course take some six or seven months. If it were only possible for us to go to Europe in the Spring or Summer, we could probably bring her back with us. But the chances for a European trip grow slimmer and slimmer. If the business goes well and we have the money to go, we wont be able to leave the business and if it doesn’t go well then we haven’t the money. As you see, a quite ridiculous situation. But don’t let me get started on Europe again- that’s just fatal.
I wrote to Charles Forberg about building a house for mother, but meanwhile she has been persuaded not to build and also it turns out that Chuck is or more or less permanently attached in Colorado and would have to do his building in California in absentia. This would be both cumbersome and expensive, so it’s just as well probably that the plans fell through. What of your own plans for the coming year? Mother tells me that you are being very successful both with teaching and make mobiles? I hope that doesn’t mean you’re settling down to be a career woman. Mutch better to follow Nan’s lead. Not that it isn’t nice to earn money independently for a while- as long as it is only a while. I wont ask you how Lucian likes going to school because I’m sure that by now he must be very fed up. But what are you intentions for later on? Teaching jobs again, or the school you were planning? Casting around from one school to another no coubt has its disadvantages, but having a school of your own brings so many worries and complexities- I wonder whether it is worth it- look what it did for the Dreiers. I still wish there were some way in which we could all do something together- I have in mind a nice quiet community, ivory towered and far from the you know what. How about reclaiming some of South America- I’ve always had a great yen for that part of the world and besides Spanish and Italian are quite similar and now that you speak Italian fluently you shouldn’t have much trouble picking it up.
My lunch hour is over and I’d better send this off instead of waiting till I have time to continue. Please answer soon and maybe even such lazy characters as you and I could learn to strike up a lively correspondence. Meanwhile don’t let the picket fences and tidy get your goat- get their’s instead- and help me make some good plans for our joint future. Love to Lucian and Bobby and greetings to all the rest.
Yours till hell freezes over Liese

title: Letter typed with envelope
credit: Black Mountain College Collection, gift of the Estate of Jane Slater Marquis
description:
Armando Dal Molin
MUSIC TYPOGRAPHERS
118 EAST 70TH STREET, NEW YORK 21, N.Y.
Dear Slatso-Fatso
You have been correctly informed by that no-account brat of an informer who has taken away the succelence and aroma of my good news. As a matter of fact I only found out very officially last week although, naturally I was quite sure long before that due to any number of symptoms such as an alarming business which I can hardly afford but on the other hand, can do very little about. Also just to break the monotony, though none of our friends seemed to have these troubles, I've been quietly (and not so quietly) throwing up not just mornings, but all day every day, but then I suppose the least thing the daughter of an obstetrician can do is to have a few obsterical complaints. Anyway, now I'm fine, having solved my stomach problems by letting Armando serve my breakfast in bed, any my only complaint is that it takes too damn long and I'm already tired of waiting out the nine months. The glorious event, by the way, is scheduled to tkae place around the first of November. If you can suggest any nice names that will sound well both in English and Italian and wont seem too foreign in combination with our very romantic sounding last name, please- all offerings are thankfully accepted, if not used.
As for sending you cookies, I'm quite aware of the fact that you don't deserve them but on the other hand I knew that was practically the only way I could bribe you into writing to me out of your smug and satisfying life. Futhermore I will shamelessly state that that was only a come-on and if you write me longer and more fully, especially as regards to your plans for the immediate future starting with this summer, I'll send you a much larger and more enticing box. Should you decide to come East, which I suppose seems fairly hopeless?! I can offer a cottage (rather primitive without water) on an island off the coast of Maine which father recently acquired sight unseen, and which we hope to take over for two or more weeks at the end of August (a plan subject to changes) also, there is a house in the process of being built out halfway on long island somewhere near Oyster Bay, with beach rights on the north shore and very few people. If the house itself is not built by then there is a small cottage standing on the property which is inhabitable. Besides which we can naturally have our living room to offer you at any time you wish to stay here in the awful city which is not especially advisable during the summer as you know. With Mrs. Dal Molin presently being in charge of the kitchen we can offer all sorts of good food I am not in the least inclined to prepare myself. What other inducements can we offer? I've also thought of getting either the Stollers or the Engels involved in the Maine deal since I'm sure the house will hold quite a few people but as far as the Stollers are concerned their baby might make difficultires. Please let me hear soon how you feel about all this.
What are you doing, or I should say planning otherwise. Because evidently your are doing more than enough now. Will Lucian be finished studying this Spring and where will you go from there? Doyou plan to live in California henceforth? If so will you build another house or are you going to start a school or join a school and how would you personally feel about that. What's this idea about going to Switzerland, or was it Sweden? It sounds wonderful in any case, I'm still yearning to go to Europe but chances look slimmer and slimmer with all the new financial strains and responsibilites. Still I'm not giving up hope- and I certainly have no compunction of packing up a family of ten and hauling them off on a trip around the world though preferably a little less primitively than Kon-Tiki (wonderfully exciting movie I thought altogether marvelous people to do such a wild and dangerous thing.)
Armando says I have to go to bed and I'd better send this off soon or I'll forget so I'll end now. Nothing much new to tell anyhow. We are still busily playing recorder (I've had to put my clarinet playing on the shelf for a while because of lack of time and money) and getting great fun and satisfaction from it. My job's the same as always, busy and full of minor headaches and squabbles. I'll be leaving there for good at the end of the summer, and not entirely without regrets. I think I learned a great deal there besides the trade itself which I hope will someday come in very handy in running the Armando Dal Molin Music Press. But then, babys are fun too in a different and even more absorbing way, and though I'm scared of the whole project, I don't mind admitting, I think I might find it even more satisfying than holding down the more glamorous responsibilites of a personal career.
Please write soon, cookies or not., especially as regards to the summer, and if you're too involved to write phone my mother and tell her. Love to you all from us all "mom" Liese

title: Handwritten letter with envelope
description:
Hoot Hoot- this life is for night owls- could if we dont stop trying to pretend we are members of the great feathered clan we'll never live to hatch another egg- much less child- Jonathan is a trap into which we fall, grinning like fools- He hasn't had a 2am feeding since he was 2 wks old. But he does have a 10pm- and since my schedule stretches in all directions to include 5 of us, this is likely to be 9, 10, 11, or 12- He is so goddamned socialable after eating- and Stone and I are only too willing to be entranced- mesmerized - one would think, from our behavior, that we had never had a baby- It's partly due to the necessary restraint when Rob and Meredith are presernt- equal opportunity- for all et- You should see our bed some mornings at 6:30- Stone, out like a light, but still grunting and protesting at the sudden increase in population- Jonathan oblivious to everything but sucking- Jane using arms like potective wing trying to ward off feet, arms, hands, cats, dogs, etc- The rest is a constantly moving mass of child flesh- the minute Rob and Meridith get on a bed they assume fish-like characteristics- the bedding becomes water for them, the bed is the bottom of the sea (they might as well- our bed is always full of sand- even though I demand "shoes off!", the socks and toes are full and they always leave it behind- hence the sandy bottom)- Jonathan will grow up thinking he never completed his ontological growth- Each child brings a new nursing experience I thought I had it after a month of Meridtih resentfully kicking my spine, but this early morning existence in a bed of eels is far more creative- sill- both Stone and I would like another- soon- next Spring- the urge to reproduce seems to increase proportionately- if the (?) kept pace all would be well- poor old Stone sweats over a hot camera, enlarges, developing (?) all day and all night- and even though he appears in neat type in those magazines, reputation is not all- on the other hand we are a - ahem- happy band of gypsies (this is to be said with a Helen Idokinson face) and after 10 1/2 years of wedded bliss we never had it so good yet- we wish you were Dr. and Mrs.- maybe it would increase our chances of seeing you- anyway- in lieu of personal appearances I scud kinder pictures- the one of Roo is lousey- and Meridith has since lost her other front tooth - but there they are- all my god three of them-
With many loves
Us Stones

title: Syllabary Pot
credit: Museum purchase with funds provided by 2021 Collectors' Circle members Kevin Click & April Liou in memory of Myron E. Click
description:
Brown ceramic pot with wavy rim and 4 short legs at base. The outer surface is decorated with a woven texture with symbols inside leaves interspersed throughout.

A syllabary is a written language in which each symbol represents a spoken sound, or syllables. The Cherokee syllabary was invented and developed by a single person, Sequoyah (circa 1776–1843) in the early 1800s. Sequoyah saw non-Indigenous soldiers reading and writing in English and wanted the Cherokee people to have a written language too because at the time the Cherokee language only existed orally. He noted that “talking leaves,” or words on paper, were a method of how one could convey thoughts non-verbally. On this pot, McCoy references Sequoyah’s idea of “talking leaves” by carving leaves with various characters from the Cherokee syllabary on them, thus making the leaves “talk.” McCoy made this work to complement another of her works, called Talking Leaves, also relating to Sequoyah and the Cherokee Syllabary.

[Source: Museum Staff]

This work is made in the style of a pigeon pot which is recognizable by its feet. While the rim of this style of pot is usually wide, McCoy likes to play with the shape of the rims on her work. As McCoy explains, “I like making this uneven rim on the pigeon pots. It makes me think of our mountains.”

[Source: Tara McCoy]

title: Cosmos, 1990
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: The crowded abstract depiction contains a lot of figures, particularly on the left side. In the upper right portion there is a monster-like figure and in the lower right portion there is a blackhole.

title: Island Idyll
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: In the foreground of the image there is a house with a chimney and trees to the left of it. In the background there is a large body of water with an island and mountains behind that.

title: Jehovah's Eye
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: The abstract image is largely made up of lines swirling and intersecting with one another in the center. There are also black and white shapes in the background.

title: Mediterranean Memory
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: The foreground of the image has a cactus on the left and stone ruins on the right witha mountain right behind that. On the left side, off into the distance a little there is a small town depicted in front of another mountain. The background is a large body of water with two fish in the upper left side.

title: Metamorphic Figure
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: The image depicts an abstract figure on the left side, seemingly flying towards they yellow and orange sun on the top right side. At the bottom of the image there is a blue mountain and above that there is a brown bird flying towards the figure. On the left side of the image there is a green serpent wiggling down towards the bottom of the image.

title: Moon Glow
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: On a black baground there is a white fence and large tree depicted in the foreground. There is a house, garage, and car depicted behind that with a person walking towards the house.

title: Noah
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: There is a black and dark blue boat in the foreground of the image with animals depicted in the bottom right corner and Noah in the center with his arms held to the sky. The boat is floating on an orange body of water during the orange sunset and there is a bird flying towards Noah with a branch in its beak in the center of the image.

title: Ozymandias [2nd Edition]
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: The image is divided into three registers and the top register has a triangular shape within it. The middle register has a black trapezoid shape that is placed diagonally and the bottom register has a triangular shape as well as two humans within it.

title: Pathos
credit: Gift of Joel Dryer
description: Black abstract blob-shaped image that occcupies a majority of the bottom left corner and center of the image. Within the blob-shape there are swirling circular lines that are continuous and add dimension to the image.

title: Zealandia Estate for Philip S. Henry, Design of Bridge
credit: Richard Sharp Smith Collection, gift of the Historic Resources Commission of Asheville and Buncombe County
description: Elevation drawing of carriage bridge on Zealdnia Estate on Beaucatcher Mountain in Asheville, North Carolina. Bridge is associated with local folk stories about a ghost.
